meta.title: Innovative Reading Pedagogies — Research Findings
meta.description: Evidence-based alternatives to the traditional receptive reading lesson (Shape E). Each pedagogy includes enough structural detail for an agent to construct new lesson shapes following the LESSON-SHAPES JSON convention.
sources: Slavin et al. (2011) — Collaborative Strategic Reading
Belkhir et al. (2025);多项 AI in EFL reviews — AI-Assisted Reading
shape_e_limitations: Teacher-directed comprehension questions — students passively answer
Single reading, single task — no strategy instruction
Comprehension is tested, not monitored or repaired
Post-reading speaking is tacked on, not integrated
One-size-fits-all — no differentiation within the lesson
meta.recommended_combination: Reciprocal Teaching (reading stage) + RADEC Create phase (output stage) — addresses Shape E's two biggest gaps: lack of strategy instruction and lack of genuine productive output.

pedagogies.name: Reciprocal Teaching
pedagogies.description: Students rotate four comprehension roles (Predictor, Clarifier, Questioner, Summariser) while reading a text in sections. The teacher scaffolds gradually, then releases control. Students take ownership of comprehension monitoring.
pedagogies.pedagogical_justification: Reciprocal teaching is one of the most robustly supported reading approaches. Meta-analyses consistently show effect sizes of d=0.32-0.88 on comprehension (SAGE Journals, 2025). The four roles make comprehension strategies visible and teachable, transforming passive reading into active strategy use. Unlike Shape E, which tests comprehension after reading, reciprocal teaching builds comprehension during reading.
when_to_use: Texts with multiple sections that can be read incrementally
Mixed-ability classes where students need different levels of support
When the goal is to develop independent comprehension strategies
B1-B2 level texts where students can discuss meaning in English
when_not_to_use: Very short texts (under 500 words) — not enough material for role rotation
Pure listening lessons — roles are designed for reading
When students are completely new to the concept and need full teacher modelling first
pedagogies.main_aim_format: By the end of the lesson, learners will have practised and applied [Predictor/Clarifier/Questioner/Summariser] strategies to comprehend a text about [topic].
key_principles: Roles rotate every section, not every lesson — with 3 sections, every student does every role once
Text is delivered in chunks, not all at once — keeps roles live
Teacher circulates and intervenes only when groups are stuck
The hardest part for teachers is staying quiet — comprehension is student-owned
Start with Summariser for first-time groups (most structured role)

predictor.description: Before reading each section, look at headings, subheadings, or pull-quotes and guess what the text will say.
predictor.purpose: Activates schema, creates anticipation, makes prediction a reading strategy
sentence_starters: The heading says... so I think the text will...
Based on the previous section, I predict...

clarifier.description: Identify what was confusing and work to fix it — with the teacher's help when needed.
clarifier.purpose: Makes it legitimate to say 'I didn't understand' and do something about it
sentence_starters: I didn't understand when it said...

questioner.description: Generate questions about the text — not comprehension-check questions, but genuine 'I wonder' questions.
questioner.purpose: Provokes curiosity, shifts from passive reception to active inquiry
sentence_starters: What questions does this raise for you?
What would you ask the author if you could?
What's the most important question this text answers?
Why do you think the author included this?

summariser.description: Write a brief summary of each section in their own words.
summariser.purpose: Forces distillation of main ideas from supporting details
sentence_starters: The main point of this section is...
In one sentence, this section tells us...

stage_template.stage_aim: To activate schema and set the context
stage_template.procedure: Splash image or statistic related to the topic. Pair discussion: 'What do you know about...?' Whole-class feedback.

stage_template.stage_aim: To read the first section with a specific comprehension role
stage_template.procedure: Assign roles (P/Q/C/S). Students read section 1 silently (1.5-2 min). Each student performs their role for the group (2-3 min).

stage_template.stage_aim: To apply comprehension strategies to a new section with a different role
stage_template.procedure: Roles rotate (P→Q→C→S). Students read section 2 silently. Perform roles. Teacher addresses 2-3 common clarifier points with whole class.

stage_template.stage_aim: To apply comprehension strategies to the final section
stage_template.procedure: Roles rotate again. Read + perform roles. This section is typically the actionable one — Summariser has the hardest job.

stage_template.stage_aim: To consolidate understanding and address misconceptions
stage_template.procedure: 'What was the most surprising thing you learned?' 'Which of the solutions will you actually try?' Teacher addresses misconceptions surfaced during Clarifier stages.

stage_template.stage_aim: To check individual comprehension
stage_template.procedure: Individual: Write one sentence summarising the whole text. OR: 'Write one question you still have after reading this.'

role_card_design.note: Keep cards simple. B1 students need more scaffolding (more sentence starters, simpler language). B2 students can handle open-ended Questioner prompts.

b1_vs_b2.b1: More sentence starters on role cards, simpler language in role descriptions, shorter text sections (~130-150 words each)
b1_vs_b2.b2: Open-ended Questioner prompts, longer sections (~200-250 words), more abstract claims in the text

research_citations: Palincsar & Brown (1984) — original reciprocal teaching study
SAGE Journals (2025) — 'Examining classroom strategies: Reciprocal teaching and its effect on reading comprehension'
Meta-analyses: d=0.32-0.88 effect sizes on comprehension

pedagogies.name: Collaborative Strategic Reading (CSR)
pedagogies.description: Students work in cooperative groups through four phases: Preview → Click & Clunk (fix-up strategies) → Get the Gist → Wrap-Up. Each phase has a specific cognitive strategy. The 'Click & Clunk' phase explicitly teaches students to detect and repair comprehension breakdowns.
pedagogies.pedagogical_justification: CSR (16 citations, ScienceDirect 2025) makes comprehension strategies visible and teachable. Unlike Shape E, which assumes comprehension is a product of the task, CSR gives students physical tools (clunk cards) to use when they hit a comprehension wall. Strong for mixed-ability classes because group roles distribute the cognitive load.
when_to_use: Mixed-ability classes where students need different levels of support
Texts with challenging vocabulary or complex ideas
When the goal is to develop self-regulated reading strategies
Extended reading tasks (multi-paragraph texts)
when_not_to_use: Very short texts — not enough material for all four phases
When students are completely unfamiliar with cooperative learning structures
pedagogies.main_aim_format: By the end of the lesson, learners will have used collaborative reading strategies to comprehend and discuss a text about [topic].
key_principles: The 'Click & Clunk' phase is the core innovation — students learn to detect when comprehension breaks down and apply fix-up strategies
Clunk cards are physical strategy cards students use when they hit a wall
Groups have assigned roles (Leader, Clunk Expert, Gist Expert, Announcer)
The teacher models each phase before groups work independently
Get the Gist teaches summarisation as a strategy, not just a task

preview.purpose: Activate background knowledge, set purpose for reading
preview.activity: Students look at title, headings, pictures. Predict content. Set a reading goal.

click_and_clunk.activity: Students read a section. When they hit a 'clunk' (word or idea they don't understand), they use a fix-up strategy: reread, read ahead, use context clues, ask a peer.
clunk_cards: Read ahead to see if it becomes clear
Look at the words around it
Skip it and come back later

get_the_gist.purpose: Identify the main idea of each section
get_the_gist.activity: Group writes a one-sentence summary of the section. Must be 10 words or fewer. Discuss and agree.

wrap_up.activity: Students write questions about the text. Review what was learned. Predict what comes next.

stage_template.stage_aim: To activate schema and introduce the text
stage_template.procedure: Introduce the topic. Activate prior knowledge through pair discussion.

stage_template.stage_aim: To set purpose for reading
stage_template.procedure: Students look at title, headings, images. Predict content. Set a reading goal as a group.

stage_template.stage_aim: To read and repair comprehension breakdowns
stage_template.procedure: Students read a section silently. When they hit a 'clunk', they use clunk cards (fix-up strategies). Discuss difficult words/ideas in groups.

stage_template.stage_aim: To identify the main idea
stage_template.procedure: Group writes a one-sentence summary (10 words or fewer). Discuss and agree on the main idea.

stage_template.stage_aim: To consolidate and generate questions
stage_template.procedure: Students write questions about the text. Review what was learned. Predict what comes next.

stage_template.stage_aim: To share group findings and address misconceptions
stage_template.procedure: Each group shares their 'Get the Gist' summary. Teacher addresses common clunks. Discuss the most interesting questions generated.

research_citations: Slavin et al. (2011) — CSR framework
ScienceDirect (2025) — 'The impact of collaborative strategic reading on EFL students with different critical thinking levels' (16 citations)

pedagogies.name: RADEC (Read-Answer-Discuss-Explain-Create)
pedagogies.description: A 5-phase cycle: Read → Answer → Discuss → Explain → Create. The 'Create' phase is the differentiator — students produce something new from the text (a summary, a transformation, a response text).
pedagogies.pedagogical_justification: RADEC (17 citations, ResearchGate 2025) is an Indonesian-developed model gaining traction across ASEAN. It addresses Shape E's biggest weakness: the lack of genuine productive output. The 'Create' phase requires deep processing because students must synthesise and transform the text's ideas into something new.
when_to_use: When the goal is to move from comprehension to production
Texts that lend themselves to transformation (argument → counter-argument, summary → opinion, fact → creative response)
When students need to demonstrate understanding through output, not just answer questions
Any CEFR level — the Create phase scales with proficiency
when_not_to_use: When the sole focus is reading sub-skills (gist, detail, specific info)
When time is very limited — the Create phase needs 8-10 minutes minimum
pedagogies.main_aim_format: By the end of the lesson, learners will have read, discussed, and created [output type] about [topic].
key_principles: The Create phase is not a throwaway — it is the culmination of the lesson
Students must transform, not just repeat, the text's ideas
Discussion happens BEFORE creation — students refine ideas through talk
The teacher facilitates discussion, not just checks answers
The output can be written, spoken, visual, or digital

read.activity: Students read the text (silently or aloud). May include gist and detail questions.

answer.activity: Students answer comprehension questions (can be MC, true/false, short answer).

discuss.activity: Pair or group discussion about the text's ideas, arguments, or implications. 'Do you agree? Why? What would you add?'

explain.activity: Students explain the text's main idea, argument, or findings in their own words. Can be oral or written.

create.activity: Students produce something new from the text: a summary, a response letter, a visual organiser, a counter-argument, a social media post, a podcast script.

B1: Write a 100-word summary of the article
Write a letter to the editor expressing your opinion
Create a social media post sharing the key finding
B2: Write a counter-argument to the author's main claim
Create an infographic summarising the key data
Write a review of the article for a school magazine
C1: Write a critical evaluation of the research methodology
Create a podcast script discussing the article's implications
Write a policy brief based on the article's findings

stage_template.stage_aim: To activate schema and set the context
stage_template.procedure: Splash image or statistic. Pair discussion about the topic.

stage_template.stage_aim: To comprehend the text
stage_template.procedure: Students read the text silently. Teacher monitors.

stage_template.stage_aim: To check comprehension
stage_template.procedure: Students answer comprehension questions individually or in pairs. Peer check. Whole-class feedback.

stage_template.stage_aim: To deepen understanding through talk
stage_template.procedure: Pair or group discussion: 'Do you agree with the author? Why? What would you add?'

stage_template.stage_aim: To make thinking visible
stage_template.procedure: Students explain the main idea in their own words. Pairs share with another pair.

stage_template.stage_aim: To transform understanding into new output
stage_template.procedure: Students produce output (summary, letter, infographic, etc.). Teacher monitors and assists.

stage_template.stage_aim: To present and evaluate creations
stage_template.procedure: Students share their creations. Peer feedback. Teacher provides language and content feedback.

research_citations: Fauzi et al. (2025) — 'RADEC (Read-Answer-Discuss-Explain-Create) as a New Learning Model in Indonesia' (17 citations)
Implementation studies in Indonesian EFL classrooms at scale

pedagogies.name: Literature Circles + Teaching and Learning Cycle
pedagogies.description: Students take on rotating roles (Discussion Director, Vocabulary Enricher, Literary Luminary, Connector, Illustrator) within a text. The TLC framework adds explicit teaching of genre structure before the circle meets.
pedagogies.pedagogical_justification: Literature circles treat the text as a shared intellectual experience rather than a vehicle for comprehension questions. When combined with the Teaching and Learning Cycle (TLC), students first learn the genre structure explicitly, then engage with the text through roles. Published in Semantic Scholar (2025) with evidence from Indonesian EFL classrooms.
when_to_use: Narrative texts, longer reading projects, reading for pleasure programs
When the goal is to develop critical engagement with texts, not just comprehension
Literature classes, extensive reading programs
A2-C1 levels — roles can be simplified or extended
when_not_to_use: Short informational texts — not enough material for multiple roles
When the focus is on reading sub-skills (gist, detail) rather than critical engagement
pedagogies.main_aim_format: By the end of the lesson, learners will have discussed and analysed a text about [topic] using [specific roles] to explore [vocabulary/structure/themes/connections].
key_principles: Roles rotate — every student experiences every perspective on the text
The text is a shared experience, not a test
TLC adds explicit genre teaching before the circle — students learn HOW texts are built
Discussion is student-led, not teacher-directed
The teacher facilitates and extends, not evaluates

discussion_director.description: Prepares open-ended questions to guide group discussion

vocabulary_enricher.description: Identifies important or difficult words and prepares definitions/examples

literary_luminary.description: Selects key passages to read aloud and discuss
literary_luminary.focus: Text structure, author's craft, important moments

connector.description: Finds connections between the text and the real world, other texts, or personal experience

illustrator.description: Creates a visual representation of a key scene, idea, or theme

stage_template.stage_aim: To teach the genre structure explicitly
stage_template.procedure: Teacher reads a model text aloud. Identifies the genre (e.g. argument, narrative, report). Labels the structural moves (e.g. introduction → argument → evidence → conclusion).

stage_template.stage_aim: To co-construct a text with the class
stage_template.procedure: Teacher and students write a text together, applying the genre structure. Teacher scribes, students contribute ideas and language.

stage_template.stage_aim: To prepare for the circle meeting
stage_template.procedure: Students read their assigned section of the text. Prepare their role (questions, vocabulary, passages, connections, illustrations).

stage_template.stage_aim: To discuss the text through roles
stage_template.procedure: Groups meet. Each student presents their role contribution. Discussion follows. Teacher circulates and extends.

stage_template.stage_aim: To share insights and address themes
stage_template.procedure: Each group shares their most interesting discussion point. Teacher connects themes across groups.

stage_template.stage_aim: To apply genre knowledge independently
stage_template.procedure: Students write their own text in the genre studied, applying the structural moves modelled earlier.

research_citations: Daniels (2002) — Literature Circles: Voice and Choice in Book Clubs
Semantic Scholar (2025) — 'Scaffolding Narrative Reading through Literature Circles and the Teaching and Learning Cycle: Evidence from Indonesian EFL Classrooms'

pedagogies.name: Extensive Reading (ER) Programs
pedagogies.description: Students read self-selected, level-appropriate texts for pleasure with no comprehension testing. The pedagogy is: read a lot, read what you enjoy, read at your level. Comprehension improves through massive input, not through focused practice on one text.
pedagogies.pedagogical_justification: The research consensus (Nation, 2017; Kim & Webb, 2022 meta-analysis, 98 effect sizes) is that volume of reading is the strongest predictor of vocabulary and comprehension growth. ER is the most divergent from Shape E: instead of one text read intensively, ER uses many texts read extensively. The form-meaning connection is strengthened through repeated exposure across many contexts, not through teacher-led analysis of a single text.
when_to_use: As a complementary program alongside classroom instruction (not a replacement)
When the goal is vocabulary growth, reading speed, and reading fluency
When students need to build reading habits and motivation
All levels — A2-C1, with level-appropriate materials
when_not_to_use: As the sole reading instruction — ER complements, not replaces, explicit teaching
When the goal is to teach specific reading sub-skills or strategies
When students have no access to level-appropriate materials
pedagogies.main_aim_format: By the end of the [program/term], learners will have read [number] books/texts at [level] and developed their reading fluency and vocabulary through sustained silent reading.
key_principles: Students choose what they read — motivation is essential
Texts must be at the right level — 95-98% comprehension without a dictionary
No comprehension testing — reading is its own reward
Volume matters more than depth — more books, more growth
The teacher reads too — modelling is powerful
Reading logs, book talks, and reading walls make the program visible

program_elements.book_levels: Fountas & Pinnell, Lexile, or graded readers (Oxford, Cambridge, Macmillan)
program_elements.reading_time: 15-30 minutes of sustained silent reading per day
program_elements.book_selection: Students choose from a classroom library organised by level
program_elements.no_testing: No quizzes, no comprehension questions, no book reports
program_elements.accountability: Reading logs (title, pages, enjoyment rating) — not comprehension checks
program_elements.celebration: Book talks, reading walls, class reading challenges, reading celebrations

stage_template.stage_aim: To read for pleasure at an appropriate level
stage_template.procedure: Students select a book from the classroom library. Read silently for 15-20 minutes. Teacher reads too.

stage_template.stage_aim: To share reading experiences and recommend books
stage_template.procedure: 3-4 students briefly share what they're reading and why they like it. No comprehension questions — just sharing.

stage_template.stage_aim: To notice and learn words from self-selected reading
stage_template.procedure: Students share 1-2 interesting words they encountered in their reading. Write on board. Brief discussion of meaning.

stage_template.stage_aim: To track reading progress
stage_template.procedure: Students update their reading logs: title, pages read, enjoyment rating (1-5 stars).

research_citations: Nation (2017) — Learning Vocabulary in Another Language
Kim & Webb (2022) — Meta-analysis of extensive reading (98 effect sizes)
McLean & Rouault (2017) — L2 silent reading norms
TESL-EJ v24 — Reading rate research

pedagogies.name: Genre-Based Reading (Process Genre Approach)
pedagogies.description: Students learn to read by learning to write. The cycle: Modelled reading → Joint construction → Independent reading/writing. Students analyse how texts are constructed (genre, moves, language features) before answering comprehension questions.
pedagogies.pedagogical_justification: Genre-based approaches (33 citations, UPM 2023) make the text's architecture visible. Instead of treating the text as opaque (Shape E), students learn to see the moves, structures, and language choices that make a text work. This deepens comprehension because students understand not just WHAT the text says but HOW and WHY it says it.
when_to_use: Academic texts, exam preparation, reading-to-write connections
When students need to understand text structure, not just content
B1-C1 levels — genre analysis requires some metalinguistic awareness
When the goal is to develop both reading and writing skills simultaneously
when_not_to_use: Narrative texts — genre-based is strongest with argumentative, informational, and procedural texts
When the focus is purely on reading sub-skills (gist, detail)
pedagogies.main_aim_format: By the end of the lesson, learners will have analysed the genre structure of [text type] and [read/written] a [genre] about [topic].
key_principles: Reading and writing are two sides of the same coin — analysing a text prepares you to write one
The teacher models genre knowledge explicitly before students analyse
Joint construction bridges the gap between modelled and independent work
Language features (hedging, cohesive devices, register) are taught in context, not in isolation
The cycle moves from other's text → shared text → own text

modelled_reading.purpose: Teacher demonstrates how to analyse a genre
modelled_reading.activity: Teacher reads a model text aloud. Labels the genre (e.g. argument, report, review). Identifies the structural moves and key language features.

joint_construction.purpose: Class constructs a text together, applying genre knowledge
joint_construction.activity: Teacher and students write a text in the same genre. Teacher scribes, students contribute ideas, vocabulary, and structural choices.

independent_reading.purpose: Students read a new text in the same genre independently
independent_reading.activity: Students read a new text. Identify the genre, structural moves, and key language features. Answer comprehension questions that focus on structure as well as content.

independent_writing.purpose: Students write their own text in the genre
independent_writing.activity: Students write a text in the same genre, applying the structural moves and language features modelled earlier.

stage_template.stage_aim: To activate schema and introduce the genre
stage_template.procedure: Display a text in the target genre. Ask: 'What kind of text is this? How do you know?'

stage_template.stage_aim: To analyse the genre structure
stage_template.procedure: Read the model text. Label the genre. Identify structural moves. Discuss key language features.

stage_template.stage_aim: To co-construct a text in the genre
stage_template.procedure: Class writes a text together. Teacher scribes. Students contribute ideas and language.

stage_template.stage_aim: To apply genre knowledge to a new text
stage_template.procedure: Students read a new text. Identify genre, moves, and language features. Comprehension questions.

stage_template.stage_aim: To write in the genre
stage_template.procedure: Students write their own text. Apply structural moves and language features.

research_citations: Hyland (2004) — Genre and Second Language Writing
UPM (2023) — 'Genre-based approaches and ESL/EFL writing: A review of the literature' (33 citations)
ERIC (2025) — 'Enhancing In-Service English Teachers' Lesson Planning Skills Using Genre-Based Approach and AI for Teaching Fiction Reading'

pedagogies.name: AI-Assisted Reading Comprehension
pedagogies.description: AI tools (ChatGPT, custom reading apps) provide adaptive scaffolding (difficulty adjusts to learner level), instant feedback on comprehension, generated questions at different cognitive levels, and personalised text simplification.
pedagogies.pedagogical_justification: AI-assisted reading is rapidly emerging (5-29 citations across multiple 2024-2025 sources). It addresses Shape E's one-size-fits-all limitation: different students can read different versions of the same text at their level, receive personalised feedback, and progress at their own pace. The teacher's role shifts from question-setter to facilitator and mediator.
when_to_use: When students in the same class have widely different reading levels
When personalised feedback is needed but teacher time is limited
When students need immediate feedback on comprehension
As a complement to teacher-led instruction, not a replacement
when_not_to_use: When students may become over-reliant on AI and lose independent reading strategies
When internet access is unreliable
When the goal is to develop collaborative discussion skills (AI is individual)
pedagogies.main_aim_format: By the end of the lesson, learners will have used AI-assisted tools to [read/comprehend/discuss] a text about [topic] at their individual level.
key_principles: AI is a tool, not a teacher — the teacher mediates and interprets
Differentiation happens automatically — texts and questions adapt to the learner
Immediate feedback accelerates learning — but must not replace teacher feedback
Teacher monitors AI interactions to ensure quality and prevent over-reliance
Privacy and data considerations must be addressed

ai_capabilities.text_simplification: AI can rewrite a text at different CEFR levels while preserving meaning
ai_capabilities.question_generation: AI can generate comprehension questions at different cognitive levels (recall, inference, evaluation)
ai_capabilities.instant_feedback: AI can check student answers and provide explanations
ai_capabilities.vocabulary_scaffolding: AI can identify and gloss difficult vocabulary for each student's level
ai_capabilities.reading_rate_tracking: AI can track reading speed and suggest appropriate text levels

stage_template.stage_aim: To activate schema and introduce the topic
stage_template.procedure: Teacher-led discussion about the topic. Set the purpose for reading.

stage_template.stage_aim: To read a level-appropriate version of the text
stage_template.procedure: Students access the text via AI tool. Text is automatically adapted to their level. Students read silently.

stage_template.stage_aim: To check understanding with personalised questions
stage_template.procedure: AI generates questions at the student's level. Students answer and receive immediate feedback. Teacher monitors.

stage_template.stage_aim: To deepen understanding through human interaction
stage_template.procedure: Teacher leads whole-class discussion about the text's ideas. Addresses misconceptions surfaced by AI feedback.

stage_template.stage_aim: To consolidate learning and set reading goals
stage_template.procedure: Students reflect on what they learned and set a reading goal for the next session.

research_citations: Belkhir et al. (2025) — 'Artificial intelligence in ESL/EFL education: Evidence from recent reviews' (29 citations)
SSRN (2025) — 'Assessing EFL Undergraduates' Attitudes Toward AI in Enhancing Reading Comprehension' (13 citations)
ERIC (2025) — 'Artificial Intelligence in EFL Education in China: A Systematic Review' (14 citations)
ScienceDirect (2025) — Multiple reviews of AI in language education
pedagogies.difficulty_to_implement: High (requires technology infrastructure and teacher training)

pedagogies.name: Close Reading with Text-Dependent Annotation
pedagogies.description: Students read the same short text 2-3 times, each time with a different analytical lens: first for literal meaning, then for author's craft/structure, then for argument/evidence. Annotation is physical (underlining, margin notes, symbols).
pedagogies.pedagogical_justification: Close reading (imported from US Common Core State Standards) replaces Shape E's single-reading model with purposeful re-reading. Each pass has a different analytical focus, building layered comprehension. The physical annotation makes thinking visible and creates a record of the reading process.
when_to_use: Short, dense texts — articles, speeches, literary excerpts, editorials
When the goal is to develop analytical reading skills
B2-C1 levels — requires ability to analyse language and argument
When preparing for exams that test critical reading
when_not_to_use: Long texts — too exhausting for multiple full readings
A1-A1 levels — annotation requires metalinguistic awareness
When the goal is fluency or extensive reading (close reading is intensive)
pedagogies.main_aim_format: By the end of the lesson, learners will have analysed a text through multiple readings, identifying [literal meaning/author's craft/argument and evidence] in the context of [topic].
key_principles: Each reading has a specific purpose — never read the same text twice for the same reason
Annotation is physical — underlining, circling, margin notes, symbols
The teacher models annotation before students do it independently
Short texts work better — density, not length, is the challenge
Discussion happens between readings, not after the final reading

annotation_system.margin_note: Brief reaction or connection in own words

stage_template.stage_aim: To activate schema and set purpose
stage_template.procedure: Introduce the text's topic. Ask: 'What do you already know about this?' Set the purpose for the first reading.

stage_template.stage_aim: To understand what the text says
stage_template.procedure: Students read the text once, silently. Annotate: underline key ideas, circle unfamiliar words. Do NOT discuss yet.

stage_template.stage_aim: To verify understanding
stage_template.procedure: In pairs, students compare their annotations. What did each person identify as key ideas? Discuss differences.

stage_template.stage_aim: To analyse how the text is constructed
stage_template.procedure: Students re-read, this time focusing on HOW the author builds the argument: structure, language choices, persuasive techniques. Annotate with different symbols.

stage_template.stage_aim: To share analytical observations
stage_template.procedure: Small group discussion: What techniques did the author use? Why? How effective were they?

stage_template.stage_aim: To evaluate the strength of the argument
stage_template.procedure: Students re-read a third time, focusing on the quality of evidence and the strength of the argument. Annotate: Is the argument convincing? What evidence supports or weakens it?

stage_template.stage_aim: To evaluate the text's argument collectively
stage_template.procedure: Whole-class discussion: Is the argument convincing? What evidence is strongest/weakest? What would you add?

research_citations: Fisher & Frey (2012) — Text Complexity: Rigorous Reading in Readable Classrooms
CCSS (2010) — Common Core State Standards for close reading
UHO (2024) — 'The Effect of the Close Reading Technique on Students' Reading Comprehension'
